description: Turn a client brief into design documents — the planning tools that map your spreadsheet solution before you build it.
content_html:
Why Plan Before You Build?

Imagine starting to build a flat-pack wardrobe without reading the instructions. You might get something standing, but the drawers would be in the wrong place and the door would open the wrong way. A spreadsheet solution is the same. Good planning means your finished product matches what the client actually needs — and it gives you a document you can refer back to during the build to check you have not drifted off course.

In the planning phase you produce design documents. These capture three things: how the spreadsheet will work (its functionality), how the user will move around it (its navigation system), and what it will produce (its outputs). All three must be visible in your plans — not just a rough sketch of one worksheet.

Key Fact

Five design tools can be used to plan a spreadsheet solution: flow charts, mind maps, storyboards, visualisation diagrams, and wireframes. Each has a different purpose — knowing when to use which one is part of good design.

The Five Design Tools

A flow chart is used to map out calculations and logic. If your spreadsheet needs to decide whether a value passes a condition — for example, whether a Saturday-job employee’s hours exceed a threshold that triggers overtime pay — a flow chart makes that decision path visible to anyone reading your design. The shapes have standard meanings: ovals for start and end, rectangles for processes, diamonds for decisions.

A mind map is useful at the earliest stage of planning, when you are capturing everything the solution might need to do. Start with the client’s brief in the centre and branch outward: data needed, calculations required, outputs to produce, users who will interact with it.

A storyboard shows the journey a user takes. Think of it as a comic strip for your spreadsheet: panel one shows the start-up screen, panel two shows the main menu, panel three shows the data entry worksheet, and so on. Annotations on each panel explain what happens when the user clicks a button or selects an option.

A visualisation diagram is a hand-drawn or sketched layout of an individual worksheet. It shows where data will sit, where labels will appear, and where outputs like charts will be placed. Annotations note formatting decisions such as font size, borders and colours.

A wireframe is a more precise version of the visualisation diagram — usually drawn to scale on grid paper or using software. It is especially useful for designing the navigation interface: buttons, hyperlinks, forms, and the start-up menu.

Different design tools suit different aspects of the plan. Use a flow chart when you need to show a calculation or decision — for example, a sports-club fixtures spreadsheet that calculates whether a team qualifies for the next round based on points. Use a mind map to brainstorm the full scope of the solution at the start. Use a storyboard to show how the user moves between worksheets. Use a visualisation diagram to sketch the layout of a specific worksheet. Use a wireframe to design the navigation interface with buttons and menus to scale.

You do not have to use every tool for every project — but your design documents as a whole must address functionality, navigation and outputs. A design that only contains a visualisation diagram of one worksheet is incomplete. The examiner or assessor needs to see that you have thought about all three areas.

Designing Functionality

Functionality covers what the spreadsheet does. A school canteen menu management spreadsheet might need to: calculate the total cost of each meal, sort meals by price, filter by dietary requirement, and flag when an ingredient falls below a minimum stock level. All of these need to be visible in your design before you open a spreadsheet application.

For calculations, a flow chart is particularly valuable. Draw a diamond for every decision your formula will make (“Is the stock quantity less than 10?”) and a rectangle for every action (“Display the warning message”). This means anyone reading your design can follow the logic without needing to look at a single cell reference.

User aids are also part of functionality. These include data entry messages and data validation rules. Designing these at the planning stage means you decide what the message should say before you worry about how to set it up. A good error message tells the user what went wrong and what to do next — not just “Input Error”.

Key Fact

Spreadsheet solutions can produce five types of output: charts, lists, invoices, reports, and worksheets. Each serves a different purpose for the client — a chart visualises trends, an invoice is a formal billing document, a report summarises data for a decision-maker.

Designing Outputs

Every output your spreadsheet produces needs to be designed in advance using a visualisation diagram or wireframe. Think about what the output is for: a bar chart comparing weekly sales figures for a Saturday job is very different from a formatted invoice for a customer. Both are outputs, but they have different layouts, audiences and purposes.

Page layout properties are part of output design: page size, print area, margins, headers, footers, orientation and scaling. If the client needs to print a one-page summary report, your design needs to show that the page is set to A4 landscape with a 1 cm margin and a footer showing the print date. These details are not afterthoughts — they affect whether the output is usable.

House style and branding belong here too. The client may want a specific colour scheme, font, or logo on every output. Record these choices in your design documents so you can apply them consistently when building.

Human Computer Interface (HCI) principles apply to spreadsheet design just as much as to any other IT product. When designing your navigation system, consider the following:

Learnability is how quickly a new user can work out how to use the solution the first time they open it. Good learnability means clear labels on every button, a logical flow from start-up to data entry to output, and instructions visible on screen without needing a manual.

Memorability is different: it is how easily a returning user can pick up where they left off after a gap. Consistent layout across worksheets helps memorability — if every sheet has the navigation buttons in the same position, the user does not have to relearn where to look each time.

Accessibility considerations include sufficient colour contrast so that text is readable against its background, and meaningful names for worksheets, buttons, and cells (not “Sheet1” or “Button3” but “WeeklySales” and “GoToSummary”). Screen tips — the small tooltips that appear when a user hovers over a cell or button — can also explain what a control does without cluttering the layout.

Layout considerations include the use of white space to avoid crowding, consistent alignment of labels and data, and the logical placement of navigation controls (typically at the top or side of each worksheet, not scattered randomly).

Designing the Navigation System

A spreadsheet with multiple worksheets needs a navigation system. This is how the user moves from the start-up menu to the data entry sheet, from there to the summary report, and back again. Every route must be planned: how does the user get to each worksheet, and how do they return to the main menu?

Design the navigation using wireframes or storyboards. Show the start-up flow: which worksheet appears first when the workbook opens, and what options the user sees. Then show every path through the system. Mark each navigation element (button, hyperlink, or form control) on your wireframe and annotate what it does. A design that simply lists “there will be a menu” without showing the layout will not demonstrate the level of planning that earns the top mark band.
exam_tip_html: In the ‘create’ question, read the scenario carefully and design your diagram for that specific situation. A generic mind map that could apply to any spreadsheet scores little. Label every element — unlabelled shapes, boxes and branches lose marks even if the diagram itself is correct. For storyboards, show the start-up screen AND the route back to the main menu — both are part of the navigation design. Annotate your wireframes to show colour, font and layout decisions: the assessor needs to see HCI thinking, not just boxes on a page.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Design documents must address three things: functionality (what it does), navigation (how users move around it), and outputs (what it produces).
  • The five design tools — flow charts, mind maps, storyboards, visualisation diagrams, and wireframes — each serve a distinct purpose; choose the right one for each aspect of your design.
  • HCI principles (learnability, memorability, accessibility, layout) must be visible in your design documents through annotations, not just assumed during the build.

practice_questions.text: State one design tool that could be used to show the logic of a calculation in a spreadsheet plan.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: flow chart / flowchart. No other design tool is specifically used to show calculation logic.

practice_questions.text: Outline what is meant by the term 'wireframe' in the context of planning a spreadsheet solution.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A structured, scaled outline of a screen/worksheet showing the precise position and size of each element, used to plan the navigation interface. Secure: A detailed layout diagram showing where elements (buttons, data, labels) will appear on screen. Developing: A plan/sketch showing the layout of the spreadsheet. Emerging: A design document.

practice_questions.text: Describe two HCI principles a student should consider when designing the navigation system for a spreadsheet solution.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per principle (up to 2). Accept: learnability — how quickly a new user can learn to use it (e.g. clear labels on buttons); memorability — how easily a returning user picks up the system (e.g. consistent button placement); accessibility — sufficient colour contrast, meaningful names, screen tips; layout — white space, consistent alignment, logical placement of controls.

practice_questions.text: Explain why design documents should show the navigation system of a spreadsheet solution, not just the layout of individual worksheets.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies navigation system AND gives at least two reasons with connectives. E.g. The navigation system shows how the user moves between worksheets, therefore the client can check every route is planned before building starts, which means there are no missing links (dead ends) in the finished solution. Secure: Identifies navigation AND gives one reason with a connective. Developing: States that the user needs to move between worksheets. Emerging: Vague reference to the user needing to navigate.

practice_questions.text: A student is planning a spreadsheet solution for a sports club that needs to record fixture results, calculate league points, and produce a formatted standings report. Describe four features the student should include in their design documents.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per feature (up to 4), each must be tied to the scenario. Accept: flow chart showing how league points are calculated from results; visualisation diagram / wireframe of the standings report layout; storyboard showing navigation from results entry to the report; design of data entry messages/validation for score fields; page layout properties for the printed report; house style / colour scheme; navigation system showing a main menu with links to each worksheet.

practice_questions.text: A student has designed a spreadsheet solution for a school canteen. Their design documents include only one visualisation diagram showing a single worksheet. Discuss whether this level of design is sufficient to earn a high mark band, referring to the three areas that design documents must address.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7–9): Sustained argument covering all three areas (functionality, navigation, outputs); identifies what is missing from the single-diagram design; reaches a justified conclusion. E.g. The design is insufficient because it addresses only the visual layout of one worksheet. It does not show functionality — there is no flow chart mapping any calculation logic or data entry messages. It does not show the navigation system — there is no storyboard or wireframe showing how the user moves from a start-up menu to data entry to the report and back. It does not show outputs — there is no visualisation diagram or wireframe for any chart, invoice or report the canteen manager would need. A design that omits any one of these three areas will limit what can be built and tested, and therefore restricts the mark the student can achieve in later topics. Secure (5–6): Covers two of the three areas with development. Developing (3–4): Covers one or two areas but with limited development. Emerging (1–2): Makes simple points about design documents being incomplete without justification.

knowledge_checks.q: Which design tool is most suitable for showing the logic and decisions in a spreadsheet calculation?
A storyboard is used primarily to show:
options: The precise scaled layout of a single worksheet
The sequence of screens a user moves through
The colour scheme and fonts to be used

knowledge_checks.q: Design documents must address three areas: functionality, _____, and outputs.
_____ is the HCI principle that describes how quickly a new user can learn to use a spreadsheet solution.
Match each design tool to its main purpose.
right: Scaled layout of a screen showing precise element positions
Shows logic and decisions in a calculation
Annotated sketch of a worksheet showing data and label placement

flashcard_questions.q: What is a flow chart used for in spreadsheet design?
flashcard_questions.a: To map out the logic and decision points in a calculation before building.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a storyboard used for in spreadsheet design?
flashcard_questions.a: To show the sequence of screens/worksheets a user moves through.
A scaled outline of a screen showing the precise position and size of each element.
An annotated sketch of a worksheet showing where data, labels and charts will sit.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the three areas design documents must address.
Name five types of output a spreadsheet solution can produce.

flashcard_questions.a: How quickly a new user can complete a task the first time they use the solution.

flashcard_questions.q: How does memorability differ from learnability in HCI?
flashcard_questions.a: Memorability is how easily a returning user picks up the system after time away.

flashcard_questions.q: Give two accessibility considerations for spreadsheet design.
flashcard_questions.a: Sufficient colour contrast; meaningful names for worksheets and buttons.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a data entry message do in a spreadsheet?
flashcard_questions.a: It tells the user what went wrong and what to do when invalid data is entered.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a mind map used for at the start of design?
flashcard_questions.a: Brainstorming the full scope of what the solution needs to do.

glossary_terms.definition: Documents created before building a solution that show its intended structure, layout, navigation and functionality.
A diagram using standard shapes (start, process, decision, end) to show the steps and logic in a process.
A branching diagram that organises ideas or topics around a central concept.
A sequence of annotated sketches that show how a user will move through a solution from start to finish.
A rough, annotated sketch of a worksheet or screen that shows the position of data, labels, charts and controls.
A structured, scaled outline of a screen or worksheet showing the precise position and size of each element.
Messages displayed to the end user when data is entered incorrectly or falls outside acceptable limits.
